title: 04. Caching: Read Through Cache
summary: Read-through is a caching pattern in which the application talks only to the cache; on a miss, the cache itself transparently fetches the value from the database via a registered loader callback, populates itself, and returns…
objectives: What is the read-through cache pattern, and how does it differ from cache-aside?
What is a loader callback, and why is it central to read-through?
What are the advantages of read-through over cache-aside?
What are the disadvantages of read-through, and when is cache-aside preferable?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Read-through is a caching pattern in which the **application talks only to the cache**; on a miss, the cache itself transparently fetches the value from the database via a registered loader callback, populates itself, and returns the value — centralizing miss-handling logic so every read site benefits from a single, consistent strategy.

Read-through inverts the responsibility of cache-aside. In cache-aside, every read site in the application must know how to handle a miss: check cache, fall through to DB, back-fill cache. In read-through, the application simply calls `cache.get(key)` and the cache abstraction owns the miss-handling — when the cache misses, it invokes a configured **loader** (a callback the application registers at startup) that knows how to fetch the value from the database. The application never sees the DB; it sees only the cache, and the cache is responsible for keeping itself populated. Real-world: AWS ElastiCache with read-through enabled (via libraries like `memcached-read-through` or Redis with `ModuleLoad` configurations), and Amazon DynamoDB DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) which is a purpose-built read-through cache — the application calls DAX's `GetItem` API, and DAX transparently fetches from DynamoDB on a miss, caches the result, and returns it. The application code is identical whether the data is cached or not, and the DAX layer handles all the policy.

The **loader callback** is the heart of the pattern. At startup, the application registers a function `loader(key) -> value` with the cache. This function encapsulates the DB query: it knows the SQL (or the DynamoDB `GetItem`, or the Cassandra `SELECT`), the deserialization logic, and any pre-processing. When the cache misses, it calls `loader(key)`, takes the result, stores it in the cache with the configured TTL, and returns it. This means there is exactly one place in the codebase that knows how to fetch a given entity — no duplication across read sites, no risk of one site using a different TTL or miss-handling than another. For example, a User service might register a single `user_loader(user_id)` that does `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?`, deserializes the row into a `User` object, and returns it. Every read site in the service — the profile page, the settings page, the recommendation engine, the auth middleware — just calls `cache.get(user_id)` and gets the same `User` object with the same TTL and same consistency guarantees.

The **advantages** over cache-aside are substantial. First, **code simplicity** — every read site is one line: `value = cache.get(key)`. No miss-handling boilerplate, no risk of forgetting to back-fill. Second, **consistency** — TTL, eviction, and miss-handling are configured once at the cache layer, not per read site. Third, **encapsulation** — the DB schema is hidden behind the loader; if the schema changes, only the loader changes. Fourth, **observability** — the cache layer can centrally log misses, measure loader latency, and apply policies (coalescing, jitter, refresh-ahead) uniformly. Fifth, **testability** — the loader is a pure function from key to value, easy to unit-test. Real-world: Netflix's internal `EVCache` client libraries provide a read-through API where services register loaders at startup; this is why Netflix engineers can change the Cassandra schema for a service without touching dozens of read sites — only the loader needs updating.

The **disadvantages** are real. First, **less flexibility** — every read site gets the same TTL and miss-handling; if one site needs a longer TTL or a different fallback, you need separate cache instances or key-prefixing. Second, **cache-layer complexity** — the cache abstraction is no longer "dumb"; it has a loader, retry logic, coalescing, and possibly refresh-ahead. This is more code to maintain, more bugs to find, and more operational surface. Third, **coupling** — the cache layer now knows about the DB schema (via the loader), so schema changes ripple into the cache layer. Fourth, **cold-start behavior** — on a fresh cache, every read misses and triggers a loader call; without warming, the cold-start period is slow. Fifth, **debugging** — when a read returns wrong data, the chain is longer (cache → loader → DB → deserializer → cache populate → return), making it harder to pinpoint. The pattern shines in services with many read sites that all want the same policy; it's overkill for services with a handful of reads or heterogeneous caching needs.

A common **misconception** is that read-through and cache-aside have different consistency properties. They don't — both serve stale data between a write and the next cache invalidation, and both have the same TTL semantics. The difference is purely architectural: where does the miss-handling code live? In cache-aside it lives in the application; in read-through it lives in the cache layer. Both can have the same stampede, staleness, and race-condition issues, and both need the same mitigations (coalescing, jitter, delayed double-delete, write-invalidation). The choice is about code organization, not correctness. That said, read-through often ends up more consistent in practice because the centralized loader makes it easier to apply uniform mitigations — if you add coalescing to the loader, every read site benefits, whereas in cache-aside you'd have to update every read site individually.

The **write path** in read-through is the same as cache-aside: the application updates the DB and invalidates the cache (or uses a write-through pattern for stronger consistency). Read-through only governs reads; writes are orthogonal. Many systems combine read-through with write-through to get the best of both: reads are simple (`cache.get`), writes are consistent (write-through updates both atomically), and the cache is always warm. Amazon DynamoDB DAX supports both: `GetItem` is read-through, and `PutItem` / `UpdateItem` can be configured as write-through so the cache is updated synchronously with the DB. This combination is the gold standard for "cache that's always correct and always fast" — at the cost of write latency, which is the subject of the next topic.

The **implementation** typically involves a thin wrapper around a cache client (Redis, memcached). The wrapper exposes `get(key)`, `set(key, value)`, `invalidate(key)`, and `register_loader(key_prefix, loader)`. On `get`, it checks the underlying cache; on miss, it looks up the loader for the key's prefix, invokes it, stores the result, and returns it. Advanced features include **per-key locking** (only one loader call per concurrent miss), **negative caching** (cache "not found" results to avoid repeated DB queries for non-existent keys), **TTL per loader** (different loaders can have different TTLs), and **background refresh** (refresh-ahead before expiry). Real-world: AWS DAX implements all of these; the open-source `cachetools` Python library and Spring Cache abstraction provide similar APIs.

The decision between read-through and cache-aside often comes down to **team structure and codebase size**. A small team with a few read sites can use cache-aside and keep the boilerplate manageable. A large team with dozens of services and hundreds of read sites benefits enormously from read-through's centralization — one loader change updates behavior everywhere, and new engineers don't have to learn the miss-handling pattern. Netflix, Amazon, and other large-scale operators overwhelmingly favor read-through for this reason: the operational simplicity of "the cache is always correct and always fast, and the application just calls `get`" outweighs the cost of building and maintaining the cache abstraction.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant App as Application participant Cache as Read-Through Cache participant Loader as Loader Callback participant DB as Database Note over App,DB: READ (application only sees the cache) App->>Cache: get(key) alt cache hit Cache-->>App: value (sub-ms) else cache miss Cache->>Loader: load(key) Loader->>DB: SELECT ... WHERE key=? DB-->>Loader: row Loader-->>Cache: value (deserialized) Cache->>Cache: set(key, value, ttl) Cache-->>App: value end Note over App,DB: WRITE (orthogonal to read-through) App->>DB: UPDATE ... App->>Cache: invalidate(key) Note right of Cache: next get() will miss,
invoke loader, repopulate ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Read-through: the application never talks to the DB. +----------+ get(key) +-------------------+ | App |--------------->| Read-Through | +----------+ | Cache wrapper | +-------------------+ | hit? | ----+----- yes | no (miss) | | | v | +----------+ | | Loader | (registered at startup) | | callback | SELECT ... WHERE key=? | +----------+ | | | v | +----------+ | | DB | | +----------+ | | | v | cache.set(key, value, ttl) | (back-fill, transparent to App) v return value Application code is always: value = cache.get(key) # one line, no miss-handling Loader is registered once: cache.register_loader("user:", lambda k: db.fetch_user(k)) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The application calls `cache.get(key)` — that's the entire read API. The application doesn't know or care whether the value is cached. 2. The cache wrapper checks the underlying store (Redis/memcached). On a hit, it returns the value immediately in sub-millisecond time. On a miss, it looks up the loader registered for this key's prefix. 3. The loader (a callback the application registered at startup) executes the DB query, deserializes the result, and returns it to the cache wrapper. The wrapper stores the value in the cache with the configured TTL and returns it to the application. Subsequent reads for the same key hit the cache until the TTL expires or the key is invalidated.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- A read-through cache that owns miss-handling via a loader callback.
- Register a loader for all keys starting with prefix.
- Read path: hit -> return; miss -> loader -> set -> return.
- Write path: invalidate; next get() will re-fetch via loader.
- Read-Through cache: application calls cache.get(key);
- The cache transparently fetches from DB via a registered loader.
- Longest-prefix match: more specific loaders win.
- Miss: acquire per-key lock to prevent stampede.

**Defines:** `ReadThroughCache`, `user_loader()`, `product_loader()`

```python
# Read-Through cache: application calls cache.get(key);
# the cache transparently fetches from DB via a registered loader.

import threading
import time
from typing import Callable, Any, Dict, Optional

class ReadThroughCache:
    """A read-through cache that owns miss-handling via a loader callback.

    The application registers a loader for a key-prefix at startup,
    then calls only `get(key)` everywhere else.
    """

    def __init__(self, ttl_seconds: int = 60):
        self._store: Dict[str, tuple] = {}            # key -> (value, expires_at)
        self._ttl = ttl_seconds
        self._loaders: Dict[str, Callable[[str], Any]] = {}  # prefix -> loader
        self._locks: Dict[str, threading.Lock] = {}
        self._mu = threading.Lock()
        self.stats = {"hits": 0, "misses": 0, "loader_calls": 0}

    def register_loader(self, prefix: str, loader: Callable[[str], Any]) -> None:
        """Register a loader for all keys starting with `prefix`."""
        self._loaders[prefix] = loader

    def _find_loader(self, key: str) -> Optional[Callable[[str], Any]]:
        # Longest-prefix match: more specific loaders win.
        best, best_len = None, 0
        for prefix, loader in self._loaders.items():
            if key.startswith(prefix) and len(prefix) > best_len:
                best, best_len = loader, len(prefix)
        return best

    def _get_lock(self, key: str) -> threading.Lock:
        with self._mu:
            if key not in self._locks:
                self._locks[key] = threading.Lock()
            return self._locks[key]

    def get(self, key: str) -> Any:
        """Read path: hit -> return; miss -> loader -> set -> return."""
        entry = self._store.get(key)
        if entry and entry[1] > time.time():
            self.stats["hits"] += 1
            return entry[0]

        # Miss: acquire per-key lock to prevent stampede.
        with self._get_lock(key):
            entry = self._store.get(key)              # double-check
            if entry and entry[1] > time.time():
                self.stats["hits"] += 1
                return entry[0]
            self.stats["misses"] += 1
            loader = self._find_loader(key)
            if loader is None:
                raise KeyError(f"No loader registered for key: {key}")
            self.stats["loader_calls"] += 1
            value = loader(key)                        # transparent DB fetch
            self._store[key] = (value, time.time() + self._ttl)
            return value

    def invalidate(self, key: str) -> None:
        """Write path: invalidate; next get() will re-fetch via loader."""
        self._store.pop(key, None)

# ---------- Demo: register loaders and read ---------- #

def user_loader(key: str) -> dict:
    """Simulated DB lookup for user:{id}."""
    print(f"   [LOADER] querying DB for {key}")
    time.sleep(0.05)                                  # 50 ms DB latency
    user_id = key.split(":")[1]
    return {"id": user_id, "name": f"User {user_id}", "email": f"u{user_id}@x.com"}

def product_loader(key: str) -> dict:
    """Simulated DB lookup for product:{id}."""
    print(f"   [LOADER] querying DB for {key}")
    time.sleep(0.05)
    pid = key.split(":")[1]
    return {"id": pid, "title": f"Product {pid}", "price": 19.99}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cache = ReadThroughCache(ttl_seconds=5)
    cache.register_loader("user:", user_loader)
    cache.register_loader("product:", product_loader)

    print("--- First read of user:42 (miss -> loader -> back-fill) ---")
    t0 = time.time()
    u1 = cache.get("user:42")
    print(f"  result={u1}  latency={(time.time()-t0)*1000:.0f} ms")

    print("\n--- Second read of user:42 (hit, no loader call) ---")
    t0 = time.time()
    u2 = cache.get("user:42")
    print(f"  result={u2}  latency={(time.time()-t0)*1000:.0f} ms")

    print("\n--- Read of product:7 (different loader, same API) ---")
    t0 = time.time()
    p1 = cache.get("product:7")
    print(f"  result={p1}  latency={(time.time()-t0)*1000:.0f} ms")

    print("\n--- Invalidate and re-read (miss -> loader) ---")
    cache.invalidate("user:42")
    t0 = time.time()
    u3 = cache.get("user:42")
    print(f"  result={u3}  latency={(time.time()-t0)*1000:.0f} ms")

    print(f"\nStats: {cache.stats}")
    print("Note: application code only ever calls cache.get(key).")
```

quiz.explanation: Read-through is a caching pattern where the application calls only cache.get(key) and the cache abstraction transparently handles misses by invoking a registered loader callback that fetches from the database. The application never sees the DB; the cache owns miss-handling, TTL, and back-fill. In cache-aside, the application itself orchestrates: check cache, on miss query DB and back-fill cache.

quiz.explanation: Negative caching means caching the "not found" result when the loader returns no value (e.g., the DB query returns zero rows). Without negative caching, every request for a non-existent key triggers a DB query — a single malformed client requesting user:999999999 repeatedly can saturate the DB.
